newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS- T-bond vols up after big Sept call buying.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS- T-bond vols up after big Sept call buying.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. Treasury bond options firmed after a large purchase of September calls in otherwise slow, listless afternoon trading, dealers said.
An investment bank was said to have bought a total of 12,000 to 15,000 contracts of out-of-the-money September 112 calls in Chicago Board of Trade T-bond futures options.
"That's been the trade of the day. That really turned vols around," said a brokerage firm trader at CBOT.
Implied volatility for at-the-money September options stood at 8.9 percent in mid-afternoon trade against 8.7 percent at Friday's close.

With the underlying bond market calmly hovering slightly above Friday's closes, despite a harrowing slide in the dollar against the yen since Friday, T-bond volatilities had been under pressure until the big call purchase, traders said.
"We took out the old high (in June futures at 110-14/32) by a couple of ticks, and that was about it for the day," a second brokerage firm trader said.
But as the market digested the huge call purchase, prices of other September options as well as some other months edged up due to hedging by market makers on the other side of the deal, traders said.
June options, which expire on Friday, saw little action, although many traders were expected to roll over their positions into July ahead of the May 20 Federal Open Market Committee meeting.
"Based on open interest in the June 110 calls, you'd think something's going to happen," the first brokerage trader said.
Open interest in June 109, 110 and 111 calls totalled 18,914, 47,978 and 31,534 contracts respectively at the end of Friday.

Even though June options do not cover the May 20 FOMC, traders said they still offered value because of their high gamma, particularly with the market facing a week loaded with economic indicator releases. April retail sales data were due out Tuesday, the April producer price index Wednesday and the consumer price index Thursday.
Shorter-dated options are rich in gamma, which gives them quicker acceleration against bond price movements.

Implied volatilities for Eurodollar futures options on the Chicago Mercantile Exchange were little changed as traders quietly awaited the data. September and December volatilities were virtually steady at 10.0 and 11.5 percent.
While the futures market looked positive from a technical standpoint, inflation data and the dollar remained wild cards ahead of the FOMC meeting, a bank trader at the CME said.

"If the numbers are benign or a little friendly, then I think it's kind of old news," he noted. "If there's a surprise, it seems like we're subject to further discussions about what the lower dollar means, inflation-wise."
